topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Concurrency can improve throughput while also adding synchronization, queueing, and scheduling costs. A bounded task pool makes those costs and its shutdown policy explicit. Harbor’s pool returns futures for results, drains accepted work, and propagates task failures without allowing exceptions to escape worker threads.

topics.title: 19.1.1 Reducing Lock Contention
topics.summary: Contention occurs when multiple workers need the same serialized resource. Reducing critical-section duration, batching updates, partitioning ownership, or using thread-local partial results can help. Replacing a mutex with an atomic does not automatically remove contention on the same shared cache line.

topics.title: 19.1.2 Avoiding False Sharing
topics.summary: False sharing occurs when independent data used by different cores shares a coherence unit, causing traffic despite no logical data sharing. Separating frequently written per-worker state can reduce it on a measured platform. The relevant line size and topology are hardware properties, not universal constants of C++.

topics.title: 19.2.1 Building Thread Pools
topics.summary: A pool amortizes thread creation across tasks. Its design must define queue capacity, submission behavior under load, exception propagation, shutdown, and whether workers may submit recursively. A bounded queue introduces backpressure but can deadlock a naive recursive submission pattern when all workers wait for work that cannot be admitted.

blocks.text: The supplied pool accepts externally submitted long-long tasks and returns futures. It is intentionally not a work-stealing runtime. Owner-thread shutdown drains accepted tasks; concurrent shutdown calls and worker-initiated shutdown are outside its contract. These boundaries are documented rather than hidden behind a generic name.

topics.title: 19.2.2 Applying Work Partitioning
topics.summary: Partition independent data so each task owns a clear range and writes disjoint output. Too-fine tasks can spend more time in queueing and synchronization than computation; too-coarse tasks can leave workers idle when work is uneven. Choose granularity using measured workload cost and variability.

blocks.text: A shared_ptr makes the wrapper copyable for std::function, even though packaged_task itself is move-only. That convenience has allocation and reference-counting costs. The example exposes those costs rather than calling the pool zero-overhead. A production executor may use a move-only task wrapper or preallocated storage after measurement justifies it.

blocks.text: Constructor failure closes the queue before joining already-created workers. shutdown closes admission and drains queued tasks before clearing the jthread vector. Calling shutdown twice from the owner thread is harmless. Calling it from a worker would attempt to join the current thread and is explicitly prohibited by the interface contract.

topics.title: Solution and review notes
topics.summary: A worker that blocks trying to submit into a full queue can occupy a thread needed to drain that queue. If every worker does so, no progress is possible. Work stealing, inline execution, reserved capacity, or a prohibition on recursive submission are different policies with different guarantees.
